clue.text: Predictably, sadly, start to unclasp purse, alas!

indicators.note: sadly here means in a sorry, messed-up state, so the letters come out in a muddled order
the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is U

explanation.surface: Someone sighs as they go to open their purse, sadly finding it as empty as ever.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'start to' unclasp is U; with PURSE and ALAS it is rearranged, 'sadly'.
explanation.definitionFit: As per usual means in the customary way, just as one would expect or predict.

clue.text: A revolutionary's a persistent pain

parts.note: the clue's first word, taken at face value
Che Guevara is the crossword's standing revolutionary, and his first name is the three letters

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s does the joining, so 'A revolutionary's' means A plus CHE is. Guevara turns up so often that the word alone is enough to summon him.
explanation.definitionFit: a persistent pain → ACHE: not the sharp stab of a twinge but the dull continuous kind of hurt, which is the sense 'persistent' pins down.

clue.text: Quiz mostly a beast

parts.note: to pump somebody is to quiz them for information; three of its four letters are wanted
the clue's own word, used as the letter it is

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiz' looks like the setter addressing you, and it is a synonym instead: pumping someone for facts is quizzing them.
explanation.definitionFit: beast → PUMA: definition by class, the big cat of the Americas also known as the cougar or mountain lion, so one animal answers to the general word.

clue.text: How to make realisation?

indicators.note: the clue asks how to make this word, and the answer, meaning reorganise, is the instruction: the letters are reorganised

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about how one arrives at a realisation.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both the method and the result: to rationalise is to reorganise, and reorganising its letters makes REALISATION.
explanation.definitionFit: To rationalise is to reorganise something more logically, which is exactly how the word realisation is produced from it.

clue.text: Activate a kind of cycle and long to swap hands

indicators.note: the hands are left and right, so the left letter is swapped for the right

parts.note: spindly means long and thin

explanation.surface: Instructions for switching on a washing machine's cycle, with a longing to swap hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The hands are left and right, L and R: 'to swap hands' replaces the L of SPINDLY with R.
explanation.definitionFit: To spin-dry is to start the washing machine's spinning cycle, which wrings water from the clothes.

clue.text: Orange licorice, somewhat divine

indicators.note: Somewhat means partly rather than wholly, so only a stretch of what is written counts, and the stretch is a run of letters.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters that pay no attention to the gap between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: A sweetshop shelf is all the surface is doing. Orange and licorice are two flavours nobody would put together, and an odd pairing of words is usually a hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: divine → ANGELIC: not the god sense but the heavenly-manner one, said of behaviour so good it might have come from an angel.

clue.text: Computer owner regularly getting bum steer

indicators.note: Doing something regularly is doing it at a fixed interval, and the interval here is one letter on, one letter off, across both words.

parts.note: count the second letter of each pair, straight through the gap, and four come out in order

explanation.walkthrough: A bum steer is a duff piece of advice, and the whole surface exists to make that phrase sound natural. Only one word here is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Computer owner → USER: the person who works the machine rather than the one who paid for it, which is the everyday sense of owning a computer.

clue.text: She regularly attended court having broken giraffe's foot

indicators.note: Something broken has to be reassembled, and letters reassembled need not go back the way they came.

parts.note: eight letters, with the apostrophe counting for nothing
ft is the standard short form of foot, as in six ft tall

explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like an instruction to take every other letter, and it is part of the definition instead: the German won 22 grand slam singles titles, so she was on court constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: She regularly attended court → STEFFI GRAF: the court is a tennis court rather than a royal or legal one, and hers was the dominant career of the late 1980s.

clue.text: Pay rock band in Paris, one wanting speed

parts.note: the Athens, Georgia group behind Losing My Religion, three letters of initials
'one' spoken in Paris is French, and the feminine form runs to three letters
the rate something moves at is its speed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock band in Paris' reads as one phrase, a group playing a gig abroad. The comma is doing the real work: Paris belongs to the 'one' that follows it, not to the band.
explanation.definitionFit: Pay → REMUNERATE: the formal verb for paying somebody for work done, the one behind the remuneration package printed on a contract.

clue.text: Bad actors smothering series — but to pull them would be painful

definitions.text: to pull them would be painful
definitions.note: This is a description rather than a substitutable noun: the setter names the answer by what happens when you pull one, and 'them' is what carries the plural.

indicators.note: To smother something is to close right over it, so one piece of the wordplay wraps completely round the other.

parts.note: a ham is the theatre's word for someone who overacts, and the plural is four letters
a string of victories is a series of them, one after another

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a box-set binge, which is the trap: 'series' here is not television but a run of things, and 'bad actors' is the theatrical insult rather than villains.
explanation.definitionFit: to pull them would be painful → HAMSTRINGS: the tendons at the back of the thigh, and tearing one is the classic sprinter's injury.

clue.text: Eleven, maybe, in swarm that's heard

indicators.note: What is heard is what counts, so you write down the spelling that matches the sound and not the word printed in the clue.

parts.note: to swarm is to teem, to be present in overwhelming numbers

explanation.walkthrough: An eleven is a football or cricket side, so the definition names the answer by the number it fields. 'Maybe' is the flag that a specific case is standing in for the general word.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven, maybe → TEAM: definition by example, since football and cricket sides field exactly eleven and the number stands in for the group itself.

clue.text: Canoodle, most of fungi spreading — hardly this!

definitions.text: Canoodle, most of fungi spreading — hardly this!

indicators.note: spreading signals the combined letters are spread out and rearranged
most of drops the last letter of fungi

explanation.surface: A tongue-in-cheek remark that canoodling among spreading fungi is hardly wholesome entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: such an earthy scene is hardly innocent fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Good clean fun is wholesome, innocent amusement, which a fungal tryst is hardly said to be.

clue.text: Bad timing?

parts.note: the reading the surface pushes: a remark made at the worst possible moment, or a comedian who fluffs the pause; the reading the setter means: timing in the historical sense, a thing placed in the wrong century altogether

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, no separable wordplay, one pun on 'timing'. A wristwatch on a Roman centurion is bad timing in the setter's sense: the object is right, the era is wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad timing? → ANACHRONISM: something belonging to the wrong period, so the timing that has gone bad is historical rather than conversational.

clue.text: Chess player getting money — that might be a bloomer

parts.note: the two sides in chess are White and Black, and White moves first
slang for money since the 1930s, alongside dough

explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is also a blunder, which is what 'that might be a bloomer' wants you to hear. Both halves of the wordplay are slang, one from the chessboard and one from the wallet.
explanation.definitionFit: a bloomer → WHITE BREAD: a bloomer is a long white loaf slashed across the top, so the definition names one example of the answer, flagged by 'might be'.

clue.text: Stumbled when given flatfish that's one-third cooked

parts.note: a flounder is a flatfish

indicators.note: one-third of the six-letter word is wanted, its final two letters, so the first four are dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then cut down to its last third

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles when served a flatfish that is only partly cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-third' of cooked is its final third, ED: COOK is set aside.
explanation.definitionFit: To flounder is to struggle clumsily or stagger, so floundered means stumbled about.

clue.text: Adventurer going to extremes with many heights surrounding?

definitions.text: Adventurer going to extremes with many heights surrounding?

indicators.note: What surrounds something sits on both sides of it, so one piece opens up and the other is set down inside.

parts.note: a height is an old word for a hill, and ground with many of them is hilly

indicators.note: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so the first and last letters are taken and everything between them is left.

parts.note: the first and last letters of 'Adventurer', in that order

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue works twice: the words that build the letters also describe the man, since the first to stand on Everest really did go to extremes with heights all round him.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue reads straight as a description of the New Zealander who reached the summit of Everest in 1953, an adventurer defined by the heights he went to.

clue.text: It'll bring your phone back to life — or is that bull?

definitions.text: It'll bring your phone back to life
definitions.meaning: the thing you plug in overnight to put the battery back
an animal that charges is one, and a bull is the beast famous for doing it

explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions with a joke in the join: the modern gadget and the animal both earn the same word, one because it charges a battery and the other because it charges at you.
explanation.definitionFit: The phone sense is the everyday one; the second leans on the other verb entirely, since anything that charges can be called one, and a bull is the standard charger.

clue.text: The writer visiting French city with Frenchman — doing this?

indicators.note: To visit is to go inside somewhere for a while, so the letter that visits is placed within the city's letters.

parts.note: Tours stands on the Loire and is the French city crosswords reach for most
the person writing the clue refers to himself as I
M is short for Monsieur, the French title

explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' means the setter, and in a crossword the setter is I or ME. The definition then points back at the surface: what he is described as doing is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: doing this? → TOURISM: travelling to a foreign city to look around it is exactly the activity the word names, so the clue's own action is the definition.

clue.text: Top musician, cellist, smeared roset

parts.note: Yo-Yo Ma is the celebrated cellist

indicators.note: smeared means smudged out of shape, so the letters are smudged into a new order

explanation.surface: A cellist has smeared rosin, roset being an old word for it, on his bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smeared' rearranges ROSET into ESTRO, after MA. Roset is an old Scots word for rosin, which cellists rub on their bows.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a distinguished musician, especially a great conductor or performer.

clue.text: Basically a menace when a little rascal scoots over

indicators.note: it comes back in further over, after the next two letters
the rascal's letter scoots off from its place in the menace word

parts.note: a threat is a menace

indicators.note: a little of a word is just its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is R

explanation.surface: A little rascal scooting about is basically a menace.
explanation.walkthrough: A THREAT is 'a menace'; its R, the 'little' rascal, 'scoots' out and goes back in 'over' EA, turning THREAT into THEART.
explanation.definitionFit: At heart means fundamentally or in essence, which is what basically means.

clue.text: Modified wonky treadle

indicators.note: Something wonky is out of true and will not sit straight, and letters that will not sit straight are letters out of their proper order.

parts.note: seven letters given whole, every one of them used

explanation.walkthrough: A treadle is the foot pedal that drives a sewing machine or a lathe, so a wonky one sounds like a repair job in the workshop rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Modified → ALTERED: both are past participles for changing a thing without replacing it, the word a tailor uses when taking in a jacket.

clue.text: It has insufficient bars — or no bar at all

definitions.meaning: the bars are the little signal-strength blocks on a phone screen
a wedding or a party is also a reception, and the bar there is the one serving drinks

explanation.walkthrough: One word, two worlds. Neither half is a synonym: each describes the same failure, once in a phone signal and once at a party, and the pun lives in 'bar'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves turn on the word reception: too few signal bars on a handset, or a party with no bar in sight, and either way it is a poor welcome.

clue.text: Blood vessel's useless, you said?

indicators.note: Saying a word hands over only its sound, so the spelling you write down need not be the spelling of the word meant.

parts.note: an effort that comes to nothing is made in vain, and the two spellings are said identically

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as 'is', joining definition to wordplay. 'Useless' is the sound to be caught, and the question mark is the setter checking you heard him.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood vessel → VEIN: the vessels carrying blood back towards the heart, so the definition is the general class the answer belongs to.

clue.text: Requests jobs that will take no time

indicators.note: To take none of something is to leave it out, so the letter standing for the next word never joins the assembly.

parts.note: jobs to be done are tasks
T is the standard abbreviation for time, as in a physics equation

explanation.walkthrough: 'That will take no time' sounds like a promise the work is quick, which is the whole disguise: it is an instruction to remove the letter that stands for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Requests → ASKS: plain synonyms as verbs, both meaning to put a question or make a request, and both third person singular.

clue.text: Everyman's introduction, meeting bishop, first of several blunders

indicators.note: meeting means joining up with, so the bishop's letters join the setter's initial
a word's introduction is its opening letter

parts.note: its first letter is E
RR, Right Reverend, is the title abbreviation for a bishop

indicators.note: only the first of the word is wanted, so everything after its opening letter is dropped

parts.note: its first letter is S

explanation.surface: The setter introduces himself to a bishop and promptly blunders, the first of several mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman's 'introduction' is E, 'meeting' RR (Right Reverend, the formal style of a bishop), and the 'first of' several is S.
explanation.definitionFit: To err is to make a mistake, so errs is a verb meaning blunders.

clue.text: Stud rinses off showing lusty quality

indicators.note: off means gone bad, so the letters are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: A stud horse is rinsed off, showing its vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' rearranges STUD RINSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Sturdiness is robust strength and vigour, and lusty means strong and full of vigour.

clue.text: Duchamp's / Arp's derisive avant-gardism, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so take the first letter of each word

parts.note: the first letters of Duchamp's, Arp's, derisive and avant-gardism are D, A, D and A

explanation.surface: An art-history description of the mocking avant-garde style of Duchamp and Arp.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcel Duchamp and Jean Arp were leading figures of the movement, so the whole clue both spells and describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dada was the early twentieth-century anti-art movement that mocked artistic convention, with Duchamp and Arp among its leaders.

clue.text: After split second, mint for mint sauce, etc

definitions.note: Mint sauce is one thing and the answer is a whole class of them: 'etc' is what does the pluralising, telling you to take the family the example belongs to.

indicators.note: To split something is to break it into parts, and the parts of a pair of words are letters free to be put back in any order.

parts.note: ten letters across the two words, every one of them used

explanation.walkthrough: 'Split second' reads as an instant of time, and the setter prints 'mint' twice on purpose: the first is fodder to be broken up, the second belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: mint sauce, etc → CONDIMENTS: mint sauce is one of the things put on the table to season a meal, and 'etc' widens the example to the whole class.
